text.en: Here begins the written record of Adam’s descendants. It goes back to the day the Elohim made the first humans: they made them in their own likeness, men like themselves.
They made them male and female, blessed them, and on the day they made them gave them their name, Adam, “human”.

Verse 1 opens a new section with *sefer toledot*, “the record of the begettings”. Genesis heads its sections with the *toledot* formula from 2:4 on, but only here does it add *sefer*, a written document. Many scholars think the chapter draws on an older written genealogy, and source critics assign it to the Priestly source.

Verses 1–2 sum up Genesis 1:26–28 in brief: the verb *bara*, “likeness” (*demut*), “male and female”, the blessing. In verse 2 *adam* is the name of humankind: “they called their name Adam” (*shemam*, “their name”). In verse 3 it is again the name of one man, as it already was at 4:25.

The finite verbs of these two verses are singular in form, as is usual when *elohim* is the subject (*asah*, “made”; *bera’am*, “shaped them”; *vaybarech*, “blessed”). The Wheel of Heaven translation renders them in the plural, in keeping with its plural Elohim.

The Messages read the likeness of Genesis 1 literally. The most skilled among the creators “wanted to create a man like ourselves, artificially” (French « créer un homme comme nous artificiellement »), and of “in our image” the Messages say: “You can see that the resemblance is striking.”

The Messages cite Genesis 5 only for the lifespans, not for this verse. Verse 1 repeats the likeness of 1:26–27 at the head of a genealogy, and read with the Messages’ comment on that creation, the line that follows descends from people made to resemble their makers.
At a hundred and thirty Adam fathered a son in his own likeness, after his own image, and named him Seth. The likeness the creators had given Adam passed to his son.

Adam lived eight hundred years more and had other sons and daughters. He reached nine hundred and thirty years, and then he died. As one of the chiefs of the first men he had been granted the benefit of the “tree of life”, which is why he lived so long.
Seth fathered Enosh at a hundred and five, lived eight hundred and seven years more and had other sons and daughters. Long-lived through the same grant, he died at nine hundred and twelve.

Enosh fathered Kenan at ninety, lived eight hundred and fifteen years more and had other sons and daughters. He too was among the chiefs granted the “tree of life”, and he died at nine hundred and five.

Kenan fathered Mahalalel at seventy and died at nine hundred and ten. Mahalalel fathered Jared at sixty-five and died at eight hundred and ninety-five. Jared fathered Enoch at a hundred and sixty-two and died at nine hundred and sixty-two. Each had other sons and daughters, and each lived the long life that the Messages explain for the first chiefs.

From verse 3 the chapter runs on a fixed formula: X lived so many years and fathered Y; X lived so many years after fathering Y and had sons and daughters; all the days of X were so many years, and he died. Ten generations lead from Adam to Noah.

Verse 3 gives Seth Adam’s “likeness” and “image”, *bidmuto ketsalmo*. These are the two nouns of 1:26 (*betsalmenu kidmutenu*), with their order and their prepositions reversed. Commentators read the verse as saying that what humankind received at its making now passes from father to son.

The Messages explain the long lives. They read the offerings of Cain and Abel (4:3–4) as food brought to the exiled creators, “who remained under military surveillance”, so as “to show their superiors that the beings they had created were good and would never turn against their fathers.” Then: “They thus obtained that the chiefs of these first men be granted the benefit of the ‘tree of life,’ which explains why they lived so long: Adam nine hundred and thirty years, Seth nine hundred and twelve years, Enosh nine hundred and five years, etc. (in Genesis V, 1-11)”

The “tree of life” is the means of long life that the creators kept from the first humans at 3:22. In the Messages’ account it was granted later to the chiefs, and the exiles obtained the grant by showing that the humans would stay loyal to their makers.

The grant was personal. Commenting on Genesis 6:3, the Messages add: “Longevity is not hereditary, and the children of men did not automatically benefit from the ‘tree of life,’ to the great relief of the authorities of the distant planet.”

Read in that light, Genesis 5 is a list of chiefs. Each generation has one named man with his ages, while his other “sons and daughters” are neither named nor given ages. Genesis itself does not call these men chiefs; the word is the Messages’ (French *chefs*).

The Messages compare the creators’ own lives with these: “Our body lives ten times longer on average than yours, like the first men of the Bible. Between seven hundred fifty and one thousand two hundred years.” They owe this to “a small surgical intervention, the biblical ‘tree of life’”.

In the Masoretic figures every death recorded in Genesis 5 falls inside that range. Of the men who die, Lamech has the shortest life, 777 years (5:31), and Methuselah the longest, 969 (5:27); Noah’s 950 (9:29) falls inside it too. Enoch’s 365 years end without a death. The Septuagint stays inside the range; in the Samaritan figures Methuselah (720) and Lamech (653) fall below it.

Mesopotamian tradition also counts long-lived figures before the flood. The Sumerian King List in the Weld-Blundell prism (WB 444) gives eight kings in five cities before the flood, reigning 241,200 years in all; Alulim of Eridu alone reigns 28,800. The Babylonian priest Berossus, writing in Greek in the third century BCE, has ten kings reigning 432,000 years, the last of them Xisouthros, the hero of the flood, much as Genesis 5 has ten generations ending with Noah.

The Genesis figures are lifespans where the king list counts reigns, and they are far smaller. Most commentators treat them as schematic numbers, and note that ages decline after the Flood, through Genesis 11 to Abraham’s 175 years (25:7) and the 120 of Moses (Deuteronomy 34:7).

The Wheel of Heaven reading takes the Genesis numbers and the king list as two memories of a real age before the Flood, when a human population lived in contact with the exiled creators. It does not use the ages as a chronology, and it does not match the patriarchs with named kings.

The ancient text forms do not agree on the numbers. In the Masoretic Text the fathers’ ages at their sons’ births add up to a Flood in the year 1656 after Adam’s creation. The Samaritan Pentateuch lowers Jared (62 and 847 years), Methuselah (67 and 720) and Lamech (53 and 653), so that all three die in its year of the Flood, 1307. The Septuagint adds a hundred years to the fathering ages of Adam, Seth, Enosh, Kenan, Mahalalel and Enoch and gives Lamech 188 and 753, which puts the Flood in the year 2242 or 2262 after Adam, depending on the manuscript; where Methuselah fathers Lamech at 167, he outlives the Flood by fourteen years.
The three lifespans the Messages cite, 930, 912 and 905 years, are the same in all three text forms.

Enoch fathered Methuselah at sixty-five. For three hundred years after that he walked about with the Elohim, living in the creators’ company, and he had other sons and daughters. His days came to three hundred and sixty-five years.
He walked with the Elohim, and then he was no longer there, for the Elohim took him. Unlike the others in the list, he is not said to have died.
The Messages do not comment on Enoch; what follows on him is a Wheel of Heaven reading.

Enoch’s entry breaks the formula twice. Where the others “lived” after fathering their sons, he “walked about with the Elohim” (*vayithallech et-ha-elohim*). It is the reflexive form of *halach* that 3:8 uses for the walking about in the garden, and that 6:9 uses of Noah, again with *ha-elohim*. Where the others end “and he died”, he ends “and he was not, for Elohim took him” (*ve-einennu ki-laqach oto elohim*).

*Et-ha-elohim* in verses 22 and 24 has the article, while “for Elohim took him” has bare *elohim*. Read with the article, the phrase can mean “with the divine beings”, and the Book of *Jubilees* takes it so: Enoch “was moreover with the angels of God these six jubilees of years” (4:21, in R. H. Charles’s translation).

*Laqach*, “take”, is also the verb of Elijah’s departure in 2 Kings 2 (verses 3, 5, 9 and 10). The two are the clearest cases in the Hebrew Bible of a man who leaves the world without a reported death.

His 365 years equal the days of a solar year, and Jude 14 counts him “the seventh from Adam”. Scholars have long compared him with En-men-dur-ana (later Enmeduranki), the seventh king before the flood in the Weld-Blundell list, who reigned at Sippar, the city of the sun god Shamash. A later Babylonian text, edited by the Assyriologist W. G. Lambert in 1967, has the gods Shamash and Adad receive Enmeduranki into their assembly and teach him divination. The comparison is the scholars’; this reading does not identify the patriarch with the king.

The Greek Septuagint renders verse 24 “Enoch pleased God, and he was not found, because God transferred him”, and Hebrews 11:5 takes up that wording: “By faith Enoch was translated that he should not see death.” Later Jewish writings, *1 Enoch* and *Jubilees* above all, make him a receiver of heavenly knowledge and tell the story of the Watchers. These books are outside the canon of the Messages, and this reading does not draw on them.

The Messages do speak of the taking of Elijah: “In II Kings, II Elijah is the guest of the creators in a spaceship that takes off and carries him away.” At the Transfiguration they show Moses and Elijah “still alive thanks to the ‘tree of life’ from which they have benefited.”
With the Messages’ reading of the Elohim as the creators, verse 24 says that the creators took Enoch, and “walked with the Elohim” describes a man who lived in their company.
A further Wheel of Heaven reading goes beyond this: Enoch left with the creators alive, as the Messages say Elijah did. Nothing in the canon says this of Enoch.

Methuselah fathered Lamech at a hundred and eighty-seven, lived seven hundred and eighty-two years more and had other sons and daughters. He reached nine hundred and sixty-nine years, and then he died.

Lamech fathered a son at a hundred and eighty-two and named him Noah, saying that this one would bring them comfort from their work and from the toil of their hands on the ground the creators had cursed.
Lamech lived five hundred and ninety-five years more and had other sons and daughters. He reached seven hundred and seventy-seven years, and then he died.
When Noah was five hundred years old, he fathered Shem, Ham and Japheth. His own end is not told here: he is the man the Flood story turns to next.

Methuselah’s 969 years are the longest life in the Hebrew Bible. In the Masoretic figures he fathers Lamech at 187, Lamech fathers Noah at 182, and Noah is 600 when the Flood comes (7:6): 187 + 182 + 600 = 969, so Methuselah dies in the year of the Flood. In the Talmud (Sanhedrin 108b) Rav takes the seven days before the Flood (7:10) as the days of mourning for Methuselah, and Rashi repeats it on 7:4.

The Messages name only the first three chiefs, cite Genesis 5:1–11 and close their list with “etc.”. Extended to the rest of the line, the same explanation covers Methuselah and Lamech, each granted the “tree of life” in his own right, since the Messages say longevity was not inherited.

Lamech’s 777 years recall the boast of the other Lamech, Cain’s descendant: “seventy-and-seven” (4:24). The two lines share more names. Cain’s line in 4:17–18 runs Cain, Enoch, Irad, Mehujael, Methushael, Lamech; Seth’s line here has Kenan, Mahalalel, Jared, Enoch, Methuselah, Lamech. Many scholars take the two lists as variants of one older genealogy.
The Messages do not comment on Noah’s naming; what follows on it is a Wheel of Heaven reading.

Verse 29 explains the name Noah (*noach*) with *yenachamenu*, “he will comfort us”, from the root *n-ch-m*; the name itself sounds closer to *nuach*, “rest”, and the Septuagint renders the verb “he will give us rest”. The cursed ground takes up 3:17, and the word for the toil of the hands, *itsavon*, is the word used there. This is the only verse of the chapter that uses the divine name *YHWH*; everywhere else the chapter has *elohim*.

Read with the Messages, this is the condition of humans outside the garden, left with “rudimentary means of survival” and feeding themselves by their own labour. Lamech hopes for relief from it in his son.
Verse 32 gives Noah’s age at the birth of his three sons but holds back his death, which comes only at 9:29, after the Flood, at 950 years.

In the Messages, when the authorities of the distant planet decide to destroy all life on Earth, the exiles, “forewarned of the matter, had asked Noah to build a rocket that was to orbit the Earth during the cataclysm”.
